title: Windcatchers: Ancient Air Conditioning
summary: How windcatcher towers cooled homes in the Middle East for thousands of years without electricity, and why architects study them today.
poll: Old building ideas can be better than new technology.

versions.title: Windcatchers: Towers That Cool
versions.text:
It is a hot day. The sun beats down. How did folks stay cool long ago? They had no fans. They had no AC.

They built a tall tower on the roof. It is a windcatcher.

The top of the tower has big gaps. They face the wind. A breeze blows in. It is pushed down. Then it fills the rooms. Ah, that feels good!

Hot air will rise. So the warm air in the house goes up. It slips out at the top. Fresh air takes its place.

Some towers send the air past cool pools first. That makes the air cool down a lot.

Windcatchers are so old! Long ago, they were built in Egypt and Iran. One town in Iran has lots. Towns on the Gulf had them, too.

In old Jeddah, homes were tall. They had big wood screens on the sides. The sea breeze came in through them.

These towers need no fuel. They just use the wind.

Now, some smart folks look at old windcatchers. They want new homes to stay cool and use less fuel.

versions.title: Windcatchers: Ancient Air Conditioning
versions.text:
Picture a very hot summer day hundreds of years ago. There were no fans and no air conditioners. So how did families in the hottest parts of the Middle East keep their homes cool?

Many of them built a windcatcher, which is a tall tower on the roof that catches a passing breeze and sends it down to the rooms below.

Near the top of the tower are tall openings that face the wind. The wind high above the ground is strong, and it has less dust than the wind on the street. When a breeze blows in, it is pushed down a hollow shaft and flows into the rooms.

The tower also uses a fact of science: hot air rises. The warm air in the house floats up and escapes through openings on the far side of the tower. As it leaves, fresh air is pulled in to take its place.

Some towers send the air past pools or jars of water first. As some of the water dries up, it takes heat with it, and the air gets cooler.

Windcatchers have a long history. Paintings from ancient Egypt show rooftop vents like these from more than three thousand years ago. In Iran, people built them for hundreds of years, and the town of Yazd has so many that it is called the city of windcatchers. Towns on the Gulf had them, too.

In Saudi Arabia, the old part of Jeddah, called Al-Balad, used a smart idea, too. Its tall homes of coral stone have big wood windows called rawasheen. They let in cool sea breezes and provide shade.

Windcatchers need no fuel and no electricity. They just use wind, heat, and good planning.

Today, some architects study windcatchers because they hope to design new buildings that stay comfortable and use much less power.

versions.title: Windcatchers: Ancient Air Conditioning
versions.text:
Imagine a scorching summer afternoon hundreds of years before electricity existed: without electric fans or air conditioners, how did families in the hottest parts of the Middle East stay cool indoors? One clever answer was the windcatcher, a tall tower built on a building's roof to catch passing breezes and send them down into the rooms below.

A windcatcher's design is surprisingly simple. Near the top, tall openings face the direction of the usual wind, which normally blows harder and carries less dust high above the street. As the breeze enters these openings, it is pushed down a hollow shaft and into the rooms, creating natural ventilation.

The tower also uses a basic rule of science, which is that warm air rises. Heated air inside the house floats upward and escapes through openings on the other side of the tower. As it leaves, cooler fresh air is pulled in to take its place, so a windcatcher can move air even when the breeze is gentle.

Some windcatchers used an extra trick. Builders sent the incoming air across underground water channels, pools, or clay jars filled with water. As some of that water evaporated, it took heat away, so the air flowing into the rooms became noticeably cooler. This idea, called evaporation cooling, is the same reason your skin feels cool when water dries on it.

Windcatchers have a very long history. Paintings from ancient Egypt show similar rooftop vents from more than three thousand years ago, and in Persia, now Iran, builders improved the design over many centuries. The Iranian city of Yazd is so famous for its towers that it is often called the city of windcatchers, and towns along the Arabian Gulf built similar towers.

In Saudi Arabia, the historic part of Jeddah, known as Al-Balad, shows related wisdom. Its tall houses, built from coral stone, have large wooden windows called rawasheen, which let in cool sea breezes while also giving shade and privacy.

Amazingly, windcatchers need no fuel and no electricity at all, since they depend only on wind, heat, and careful design. Modern air conditioners, on the other hand, use huge amounts of electricity.

Today, architects are studying windcatchers with new interest. By mixing traditional ideas with modern materials, they hope to design sustainable buildings that stay comfortable while using much less energy, showing that ancient engineering can still help people solve modern problems.
